newsitem.title: USA: U.S. ruled owner of disputed oil lands in Alaska.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ruled owner of disputed oil lands in Alaska.

text.p: The Supreme Court ruled on Thursday for the U.S. government in an 18-year dispute with Alaska over ownership of environmentally sensitive submerged lands rich in oil off the state's Arctic coast.

The justices said the U.S. government, not the state, owns the coastal submerged lands that are key parts of the National Petroleum Reserve and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, two major federal reservations along Alaska's North Slope.

At stake in the long-running legal battle was more than $1.4 billion in oil and natural gas revenues from the disputed lands, money that now may go to the federal government. The case began in 1979 when the federal government filed a high court request to bring the complaint.

The state did not oppose the move and the court named a special judicial officer, who held hearings and issued a report. The federal and state governments then filed various objections to the 15 key recommendations in the report.

"We overrule Alaska's exceptions" to the report, Justice Sandra Day O'Connor said for the high court in the 62-page opinion. "In sum, we conclude that the United States did not transfer to Alaska submerged lands with the Arctic National Wildlife Range at statehood," she said in upholding the key U.S. objection to the report's recommendations.

The state unsuccessfully argued that the U.S. government did not go through proper procedures to keep the lands so they became Alaska's under a law that grants coastal states title to submerged lands extending three miles (4.8 km) out to sea.

Environmental groups, backing the federal government, feared Alaska would promote oil production along the coast of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, which they said would imperil wildlife and ruin the pristine wilderness.
